subsubtopic: CALL FOR REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last spring the Canadian Agriculture Export Corporation, Canagrex, started to serve Canadian farmers by assisting them to sell their products in the international markets of the world, and during several months of operation it has succeeded very well, closing some $16 million worth of sales, with an additional $100 million of transactions expected by March 31 of this year. It is very impressive, especially when we note the start-up costs were only $2.66 million.
In the years ahead we will see very competitive selling of farm commodities in the international markets of the world. The United States will be much more aggressive in marketing its farm products abroad, especially with the pressures expected from the new United States farm Bill.
The Government's decision to wind up Canagrex is very shortsighted. It is firmly opposed by many farm organizations, including the 300,000 member Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers Union. Killing Canagrex is like shutting down the sales department of a company wanting to expand its sales.
Canagrex has all the power it needs to help sell our farm commodities abroad by providing farm financing packages, insurance, marketing, analysis, promotion and, most of all, a one-stop selling agency far foreign buyers.
I call on the Government to reinstate Canagrex, in the name of thousands of farmers who want this corporation retained so it can get on with the job it was designed to do.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House the occasion of the 67th anniversary on January 22, 1985, of the proclamation of the independence of Ukraine.
As a Canadian of Ukrainian descent I want to join with hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian Canadians to acknowledge that the struggle for freedom and democracy may always continue.
Following the fall of the Tsarist empire on January 22, 1918, the Ukrainian Parliament proclaimed and established the independent National Democratic Republic of Ukraine.

January 23, 1985
The Ukraine recognized the highest principles of democracy, of freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly, association, and basic human rights.
However, in 1922 the Russian communist regime subverted and conquered this new independent state by force. The Communist regime was more despotic and oppressive than the Tsarist empire.
Today, the spirit of the Ukrainian nation survives. The Ukrainians have paid the price for the pursuit of freedom. History has often forgotten the Black Famine of 1933. More than six million innocent people, victims of Communism, died unmercifully through forced starvation.
We pray that freedom and human rights will always be the hallmark of our nation, Canada. We pray for freedom in other lands, for oppressed people, including the oppressed people in the Ukraine.

subsubtopic: STUDY OF AMERICAN PROGRAM
speechtext:
From January 8 to 10, Mr. Speaker, along with a group of Canadian parliamentarians, I went to Washington as guest of the parliamentary exchange centre to study their agricultural bond program and draw inspiration from their experience. This program was launched about four years ago.
We were welcomed by Minnesota representative Jim Obe-star and his wife who is on staff at the interparliamentary exchange centre. Our visit had been arranged here by Mrs. Barbara Reynolds.
I would like to say publicly just how much I came to appreciate the work and generosity of our hosts who spared nothing whatsoever to make it easier for us to learn all about this program.
We also had an opportunity to meet and discuss with the American Agriculture Secretary of State and to find out for ourselves that the problems experienced by the American agricultural community are practically the same as ours. I
I want to thank all those people for everything they did for us and I can assure them that is was a worthy experience for their Canadian guests.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF DOLLAR COIN ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is time that Canada introduced the dollar coin. Recent public opinion surveys have indicated that Canadians desire such a coin. Various vending machine companies have urged the Government to move quickly in this area, as a dollar coin would greatly simplify their operations. In this day and age very little can be purchased for less than a dollar. Bus fares in many Canadian cities exceed a dollar, while parking meters and newspapers are fast approaching that figure.
A dollar coin would be more durable than the paper dollar with its short lifespan. It has been estimated that the federal Government can save up to $300 million over a ten-year period by moving to a dollar coin. In addition, a dollar coin is lighter than four quarters.
The introduction of a dollar coin would have a significant spin-off benefit to single industry mining communities. In the riding of Nickel Belt, Inco has the capability of producing the dollar coin, and in fact such a move would create hundreds of new jobs in this community which is experiencing an unemployment rate of over 15 per cent. If the demand for dollar coins were to improve, nickel producing communities would benefit from this innovation.
I urge the Government and the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre), in particular, to move as quickly as possible to establish the dollar coin in Canada.

subsubtopic: FOOD BANKS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many Canadians from coast to coast who carry with them the haunting images of the Great Depression. They remember well the long line-ups of dispirited men and women silently waiting their turn for a bowl of soup that might stave off hunger for another day.
It is a sad commentary on the priorities of our Governments that the soup kitchen has made a dramatic come-back. In British Columbia the community food bank is now a major growth industry. In Vancouver the food bank has doubled in size in one year and it now serves over 3,000 bags of groceries per week. Yet this week it will have to turn away at least 500 people.
In Kamloops the food bank serves over 2,400 families per month. A typical food hamper for one family for one month consists of 6 cans of soup, 2 cans of vegetables, a can of fruit, a package of oatmeal, a package of powdered milk, a bag of potatoes, some Kraft dinners, 2 cans of pork and beans, a
January 23, 1985

package of lunch meat, a package of sugar, a half pound of margarine, 2 loaves of bread, and a pound of hamburger.
This is emergency assistance for one family for one entire month. It is disgraceful. This is the product of Mr. Bennett's restraint program. This is not the new reality. It is simply the old Depression. Let no one be fooled. Mindless restraint is a recipe for economic and social disaster. That is the reality the people of British Columbia know only too well, and I hope it does not now happen on a national scale.

subsubtopic: NEED FOR REFORESTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each Member in this place is no doubt aware of the dismal forecast regarding the forest industry. Our valuable timber is being used at a rate much greater than it is being replaced.
The forest industry, which is the largest employer of any in Canada, faces virtual extinction in this generation if steps are not soon taken.
The Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) is doing an admirable job of consulting with forces within the industry. However, he cannot do it alone.
We, as parliamentarians, must rise to the occasion if our most valuable resource is to be preserved. Some politicians in Canada have gained a reputation for short-sightedness and self-service. Perhaps we in this Parliament can be remembered
in history for our responsible planning for the future.
Roughly one million people are directly and indirectly employed in forestry related jobs, and their future depends on the wisdom of the present.
The replanting, weeding, thinning, and fertilization of logged land is sadly lacking proportionately to the harvest. It is bad enough to use non-renewable resources with wild abandon, but to ignore the disappearance of this renewable resource is truly criminal.

subsubtopic: REFINANCING OF LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on an issue of concern to many farmers. Approximately 1,300 farmers from the Province of Saskatchewan had been locked into high interest rate loans through the Farm Credit Corporation. It came as good news last week when the Minister of Agriculture announced that these borrowers can now have their loans refinanced at 12.75 per cent.
This measure will mean a benefit of over $3 million a year for five years to the Saskatchewan economy. It will lessen the
Oral Questions
high cost of credit. Further, it will give some farm borrowers who are facing foreclosure the opportunity to remain viable.
I would like to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), and further urge him and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to help improve the plight of farmers by introducing the removal of capital gains tax on farm land and the use of agribonds to provide low interest farm loans.

subsubtopic: STUDENT LOANS AND UNIVERSITY TUITION FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government's record on behalf of the students in this country is nothing-nothing short of appalling. It has done nothing for our unemployed youth at the very time when our young people are counting on a post-secondary education to improve their chances for employment. Many are even staying in school because they can't get jobs.
And what do the Tories do about this? The Finance Minister announces that they are cutting $5 million out of their budget and putting a freeze on the level of student loans. This will not only make it more difficult for our young people, it will even deny some of them the necessary funds to stay in school.
And as if this wasn't bad enough, the Tory Treasurer of Ontario calls for university tuition fees to be hiked by 13 per cent a year, and the Tory Ontario Minister of Education set up the Bovey Commission with both hands tied behind its back when, she said to the Commission, "Don't spend the province's money but go ahead and sock it to the kids"-so the report recommends hiking student fees by 50 per cent.
What a bind for our young people caught in this Tory squeeze play, with the federal Tory Government freezing student loans, and the provincial Tory Governments raising student fees. In this, the International Youth Year, it would have been fitting to give more to our youth, not less. The Tories truly should be ashamed.

Member would call the CBC in Calgary rather than the gentleman who was alleged to have made the statement. Mr. Speaker, I did my checking in light of what the Prime Minister himself had to say. He told the House, as did the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, that Mr. Morgan did not say what the CBC, in a nation-wide radio broadcast, said that he said. I thought it entirely appropriate, since the Prime Minister-
With great respect-

Member in his submission has suggested, and he suggests again in the words he has presented to me, that there may have been a breach of budgetary secrecy and that private commitments may have been made by the Government to representatives of the oil industry. speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government has failed to provide for significant Canadian participation in the International Year of Youth by neglecting to prepare and to put into place comprehensive job training and employment opportunity programs designed to enable young Canadians to find useful and meaningful employment and to contribute to the future of our country.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the International Year of Youth and I have in my hand the document published by the Minister representing Canada's participation in that year. I think it gives us an excellent opportunity to focus in this House on the problems facing the young people of Canada.
The three themes set forth for the International Year are those of participation, development and peace. Those themes, to which young people in this country can subscribe, are thoroughly endorsed by those of us on this side of the House, in this corner of the House. This motion gives us an opportunity this afternoon not only to highlight the problems facing our young people in Canada, but also to invite the Government to find some real solutions.
I agree with the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) when she said in this House on Monday that there is no such thing as monolithic youth. Our youth are diversified. She did not spell that out, but obviously when we speak of our young people we are talking about 15-year-olds on the one hand and couples in their 20's with a child or children on the other. We are talking of those in school and those out of school. We are talking about high school drop-outs and those who have had or are having the opportunity and advantage of a university education. We are talking about our unemployed and those young people who have an opportunity for a job either full-time or part-time. Again, we are talking about those who work on our farms and those who live in the cities, towns and villages of Canada. The one concern which overrides all others, Mr. Speaker, is the question of employment. That is the focus of this particular debate.

January 23, 1985
Supply
The total of our unemployed in Canada now rests at 1.4 million people, or 10.8 per cent of the workforce. In the age group 15 to 24 that percentage rises to 16.7 per cent, or over a half a million young people. We can pinpoint the statistic even more accurately. Thirty-six per cent of all unemployed persons in our country are between the ages of 15 and 24.

This is an incredible tragedy for our young people. It also roses a challenge to our country and to all Canadians, not only a challenge but an obligation to act. All Members of this House, Mr. Speaker, whatever their party affiliation, are daily receiving requests for assistance from young constituents. We must make it possible for our young people to have a normal life in our society, otherwise they may well be doomed to spend the rest of their lives either unemployed or on welfare, with no hope for the future.

We risk having in this country a climate of despair where our young people will lose hope, ambition and their confidence and dignity. The Government has given us fine phrases since it assumed office. It has given us great rhetoric, but its actions speak volumes for its inability to accept unemployment for youth as a major issue. It has done nothing less than savage the youth employment programs since it assumed office. One of its first acts as a government was to eliminate the First Chance program. This was a program to meet a conundrum or a catch-22 situation whereby our young people go to a prospective employer and ask for a job. The employer says: "Fine, young lady, fine, young fellow; your marks are good. You have worked hard. I like your community involvement, but you have no experience". The young person says to the prospective employer: "How, sir, can I have any experience? I have not had a job. It is my first opportunity".
We have this tragedy in our country of half a million young people with no experience and, therefore, with no job. Until they get a job, they cannot have any experience. That was the reason for this First Chance program, to give our young people a first chance by on-the-job training.
Hear, hear!

The program was announced and implemented. We were seeking the co-operation of the provinces, of labour and of business. The program was endorsed by the Canadian Labour Congress, by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, by the Chambers of Commerce across the country, by the Business Council on National Issues, and by the Canadian Federation of Labour. It addressed the crying need of young people to get their first chance and some experience to qualify them for a job.
What did the Government do, Mr. Speaker? It cancelled the program and substituted a pilot program-I see the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is here- for three or four thousand young people. It was a pilot project only. This program would have filled a gap for those who do
not go on to university to give them some training and experience to get the jobs of the future.
I have looked at the Government's paper which it produced in December, 1984. That paper argues forcefully for the necessity for a school-to-work transition program like First Chance. One turns to page 24 of that document entitled "Training" and reads:
The second strategy would follow from the view that, in a time of spending restraint, federal expenditures should be increasingly shifted to those areas where the need for federal support is clearest-
It goes on:
The result of this view would be to place greater federal emphasis on training related to the school-work transition, training for the unemployed and special groups, and training related to major career shifts.
We agree totally with the Minister's paper. We agree also with what the Minister for Youth said two days ago in this Chamber. Here are her words:
We must attempt to break down the prejudices against young people and encourage our partners in the business and labour communities to make their fields more accessible to them.
We could not agree more. What happened? The Tories axed the very program that would have done that. If the Minister for Employment and the Minister for Youth are worried about the political credit for this program, they should change the name. We could help them find a new one.
That is what they will do.
Oh, oh!
We will even relinquish the pride of authorship because it is more important for the young people to have this kind of a program.
Hear, hear!

There is no more startling proof of the need for training programs like First Chance to ease the school-to-work transition than to look at the unemployment rates of young people who have a grade eight education or less. I should like to refer to the December, 1984 figures from Statistics Canada showing those young people with only grade eight education or less as a percentage of the unemployed in the country, 30.4 per cent; with only a high school education as a percentage of the unemployed, 18.4 per cent; with some post-secondary education, 11.6 per cent of those unemployed; with a university degree, 9.3 per cent of those unemployed. Those rates are unacceptably high in all areas, but they show clearly the need for a long-term commitment by the federal Government to training programs for young people. Those statistics are absolutely convincing. That is a great challenge for the country. There is a great need to have just as strong a commitment to early school-leavers as to traditional support for those who go on to post-secondary education.
January 23, 1985

I should like to give some other examples of the attack by the Government on programs for youth. Last summer, Summer Canada provided 89,000 jobs for youths and students. What did the Government do? It eliminated that program. What about Katimavik? It reduced expenditures for that wonderful initiative by $20 million. Earlier this afternoon my colleague asked a question in the House about there being $5 million less this year for student loans. Where is the commitment of this new Government to the young people of Canada? Where is the promise for them of more jobs and a better future? I submit that, like so many other commitments and like most of the promises made by those on the Government side before they came through the curtains, entered the Chamber and sat on Your Honour's right, it has vanished and no longer exists.
What we see here is a fundamental difference in philosophy. The Progressive Conservative Party wants to rely totally on the private sector. We agree that the private sector, particularly small business, is from where most new jobs will come. However, what about those regions with no strong private sector? How does the 18 year old boy or girl in rural Newfoundland with no high school education find a job? The unemployment rate in that category in Newfoundland is 57.9 per cent. The Government is abandoning its role in direct job creation. [Translation]
In my first speech in the House, Mr. Speaker, I explained the principle of Liberalism. We believe in the private sector. We do. But the Government also has a role to play in the labour market when the private sector cannot or will not absorb the demand for jobs.
That is why we have direct job creation programs. According to another principle of Liberalism, equal access to training is essential to enable people to apply for the jobs available. However, equal access is useless if there are no programs available. That is what the situation will be as a result of the direction being taken by this Government today.

This is why we have chosen to draw this subject to the attention of the House and the country. This is why we in the Liberal Party in this quarter of the House will fight the destructive policies of the Government on training programs. I see the Minister smiles.
She laughs.

There are a half million young people in the country who should see that smile; she is laughing now.
Again the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) talked today about consultation, consensus and review. It is now clear that when the Government talks about review, it is little more than a code word for search and destroy. Young people need some help in starting their own businesses. This is why we created the Young Entrepreneurship Program. What happened to that
Supply
program? It was scrapped. The Government is abdicating its role. How can we expect the private sector to do the job on its own, particularly in the field of training and retraining? The Government is eliminating employment and training programs willy-nilly, and we have not seen any alternatives.
I ask both the Ministers who are sitting here this afternoon: Where is that plan of action? Quite frankly I do not care if they change the names of the programs or find some other epithet for them. We will sit back and let them take some credit, but they should just restore some programs for the younger people in the country who are crying for jobs.
Hear, hear!

The Prime Minister is now taking credit-don't we all notice it-for the creation of
100.000	jobs since September when he formed the Government. He knows as well as I do-perhaps he does not-that there are time lags in economic policies. Economic policies introduced by any Government take 6, 9, 12 and 18 months sometimes to bear fruit. When he recites those figures, he is just reciting the effects of Liberal policy. Even on the basis of the figures themselves-and one of my colleagues has handed me some numbers from Statistics Canada-in the last three months of the administration of Prime Minister Trudeau the increase in employment was 32,000 people per month. During the three months I had the honour to lead the Government, the figure rose to 33,000 new employed per month. Since the Conservative Government took office, the number has been
26.000	per month. Let us not play games with numbers. It does not help people who do not have jobs. It gives the Prime Minister and the Ministry a little glow of undeserved satisfaction.
With the exception of placing over 100 party faithful in patronage positions after the House rose for Christmas, adding 700 policemen to the Unemployment Insurance Commission and hiring political commissars at 80 grand for each one of the Ministers, all 40 of them-and it is the largest Cabinet in Canadian history-there has not been a single program created by the Government for direct jobs since it took office.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, I have heard that deep voice before; you know what his former Leader, Mr. Diefenbaker, used to say about voices like that.
Because I think it is relevant, I want to turn briefly to federal Government funding for post-secondary education. At the moment the arrangement is a block funding agreement whereby cash and tax points are transferred to the provinces. I can speak in my capacity as Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra in which the University of British Columbia with its
35.000	students is located. The people of British Columbia- and I am sure the people of other provinces-are concerned, as we discovered during the election campaign, that the moneys transferred by the taxpayers of Canada through their federal

Government to the provinces under post-secondary financing are not being used by most provinces for the purposes for which the funds are transferred. In British Columbia the figure is about 12 per cent. In Nova Scotia and Ontario the figure is somewhat less but still acute. The Government has not told us how it plans to renegotiate the agreement with the provinces to ensure that money destined for post-secondary education is used for post-secondary education, for research, student loans, grants and bursaries, and for a national standard so that our students can move freely and receive the same quality of education from one end of the country to the other.
I ask the Ministry-and perhaps it is the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) one should ask-what the standards will be. How will the Government in renegotiating those agreements ensure the national criteria that moneys destined by the taxpayers of the country are really spent by the provinces for the purpose of post-secondary education? Is the Government planning reductions in these transfers? I would be interested in sitting like a fly on the wall to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson); perhaps we just have to wait for the tape. Who knows? I would be interested in knowing what those conversations are. That will indicate quite clearly this Government's commitment to youth and youth programs because that formula is up for renegotiation this year. Does it agree, for example, with the Bovey report mentioned by one of my colleagues, commissioned by the Province of Ontario, which recommends a doubling of tuition fees for students so that the students themselves pay up to 25 per cent of university administration costs? What is the view of the Government?
We need a full debate in this House, and I hope the Government gives us the opportunity-otherwise we may exercise our rights in an Opposition day in the future-to debate the renegotiation of this transfer formula.
Hear, hear!

I spoke about it since my return to public life because I am very concerned that the dollars put by the people of this country into post-secondary education are not diverted by the provinces of Canada.
Members on all sides of the House, particularly those in the Liberal caucus who brought this motion before Your Honour and wish to speak this afternoon, and we as a nation, must be prepared to invest in young Canadians. We must be prepared to offer our younger citizens the chance to build better and lead more productive lives. We must replace the despair of a generation with hope. We must not lose a generation in this country for failing to respond to their needs. The meat cleaver approach taken by this Government to existing programs for youth is counter-productive to that renewal approach. Our young people do not want to hear the words "cut, cut, cut".
The Minister of State for Youth said on Monday that youth is one of Canada's untapped resources. We agree. However, I submit that the attitude and actions of this Government to date are an unqualified guarantee that Canada's youth will
remain an untapped resource this year, next year and for many years to come.
I have outlined on behalf of this Party, and I will be followed by my colleagues, areas where urgent action is required now, today. Not next month or next spring, now.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief question for the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner). In 1981, a parliamentary committee of this House reported to the House a document entitled "Employment Opportunities for the Eighties". The committee was chaired by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). I was Vice-Chairman. One thing that has disturbed me for the last three years is that so little of the advice which that committee gave to the Government was accepted.
In the context of the debate on the motion today, I would like to read recommendation 135 and ask the Leader of the Opposition whether he supports that recommendation. I think he is aware that if he does, he is essentially supporting the comments of the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) about what this Government intends to do, which is to accept advice which comes from the consultative process. Recommendation 135 reads:
The federal Government should continue summer employment programs for students, but they should be simplified, better designed and better coordinated with educational and training programs. To the greatest extent possible, the summer job program should provide additional on the job training for those who are in high school, community college or university.
That was our recommendation in 1981. The Liberals did not accept it then. Do the Liberals accept it today?
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is just reinforcing what I had to" say, and I thank him.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. In the last number of months he has travelled across this country, particularly in western Canada, and has had discussions with individual interest groups from Atlantic Canada, particularly the less fortunate areas of the country. Does he agree that it is incumbent upon the present Government, particularly the national Government, to provide some economic stimulus over and above what it may give to other areas in order to create jobs, not only for our young people but for older workers as well? Will he agree
January 23, 1985

with this sentiment that I am expressing and which has been expressed by other individual Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, with his usual perception, the Hon. Member has put it with even more eloquence than I could summon. When we talk about training, although the scope of the motion limited it to our young people because of our concentration this afternoon on International Youth Year, training and retraining is just as serious for the men and women of this country who, through no fault of their own, have been displaced by new technology, new machines, computers, the information processes or a robot. I echo the Hon. Member's sentiments very strongly.
There is another part to the Hon. Member's question. It is clear that this new Government has abandoned what was fundamental to previous Liberal administrations, that there should be equality of opportunity in this country, regional equality. There should be the opportunity for every young man and woman in every part of this country to have an equal chance at a job, whether they live in Cape Breton, from which the Hon. Member hails, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Northern Ontario, the Gaspe or Western Canada. That is a principle which we will reaffirm on another day before Your Honour when we are given the opportunity.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am wondering if the Leader of the Opposition had a chance to look at the Fiscal Arrangements Act which was amended last year whereby his predecessor forced six and five on education transfers, despite the serious opposition by this Party and the New Democratic Party. Did he look at the amendment produced in that debate by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) which specifically demanded that the Government annually file an accounting as to how the education transfer for post-secondary education was spent by the provinces to ensure that the transfer by the Government was not being used for other purposes? That amendment was put by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. Eventually the last Government was forced or embarrassed into accepting it. Has the Leader of the Opposition had a chance to look at those debates?

As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I have. Because of the exigencies of the election campaign, I even had the misfortune and burden of having to read some of the Conservative documents on the subject. I hope the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) will remind the Member for Kingston and the Islands, now the Minister of Employment and Immigration, of the words in that amendment when she and her colleagues come forth to renegotiate those agreements.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) could inform the House whether he was not surprised when, in answer to a question I

I imagine the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is aware that in view of technological change, if our young people are to have jobs, they must be able to get training. I would like to hear the Hon. I must admit to you, Sir, that in this House one always takes great satisfaction from hearing the boos coming from Members of the Liberal Party. One realizes then that one is doing something right.
I would like to begin my remarks today by saying that I express my appreciation to the House Leader of the New Democratic Party who because of my schedule made it possible for me to take part in the debate at this time by forgoing his Party's position in the debating order. I wish to thank him for that.
I also want to express my appreciation to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) for having placed the resolution before us today. I would like to tell him that I am grateful for this for two reasons. The first of these is that it reminds the House once again that, as far as the Leader of the Opposition is concerned, expediency takes preference over addressing the real needs of the nation. Second, it gives me the opportunity once again to outline the steps that we are taking to begin to redress the legacy of despair that was left to the people of this country, including young people and older workers from coast to coast, by the former Government.
The Leader of the Opposition has placed this resolution before us and he did so just a couple of days after I had told him and others in the House that there would be programs announced for summer youth within a very short period of time. Of course, what I noticed about his remarks today was his selective memory. I realize that he has been out of the

January 23, 1985
Supply
House for some period of years and I can understand why he has forgotten that, as Minister of Finance, he did not see fit to come to this House for any discussion of the Fiscal Arrangements Act with the provinces prior to the time they were negotiated. That goes back a long time. I can see why he was unaware of the debate that took place on post-secondary education in this Chamber and the amendment that I moved to look at the accountability question with the provinces. He was out of the Chamber at that time so obviously he was not aware of what happened. However, I fail to understand how his selective memory is applied to events which have taken place since he returned to the Chamber.
The Leader of the Opposition made some reference to the fact that nothing has been said about job creation or training. I am sure he would have listened with interest to the remarks made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his economic statement of last November. At that time the Minister said:
We are committed to providing lasting jobs for all Canadians who want to work. The Government will therefore be committing an additional $1 billion in 1985-86 primarily to help Canadians to acquire new skills and to find jobs in the private and public sectors.
That kind of selective amnesia which causes the Leader of the Opposition to leap over the assignment of $1 billion this year to training, human resource development and the development of jobs in all parts of the country is what I consider to be the utmost in expediency and is just an attempt to mislead the country.
It is on the question of unemployment and training where the Leader of the Opposition goes badly off the track. That is not what the people of Canada want to hear. The people of Canada know that the new Government is tackling a whole host of problems, a legacy of problems that was left to it by the former Government. I would like to say that, as far as human resource development is concerned, this Government will make an impact on the economy with which the former Government would not come to grips or begin to address, particularly in a sector that is our greatest resource, our young people.
The Leader of the Opposition commented on the training paper I tabled in the House of Commons. I am glad that he was able to comment on it today and comment on it so favourably. The last time the subject of my training paper was raised, he had not read it, he had not seen it and I do not think he even knew that it was tabled. He is coming along. He is beginning to come to grips with the subject. I am pleased to see the interest that he is taking in this.
However, in his remarks he said that the way to approach this subject is simply to change the names of the programs. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, that is not what we intend to do. We are going to take a new approach to this question. I have said that in the Chamber and I will continue to demonstrate it throughout the year and the Government will demonstrate it as it has demonstrated it already over the past months.
The Leader of the Opposition might scoff and belittle the addition of 100,000 new jobs to the economy since last fall. However, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that that means that there are 100,000 people who are working at this time who
were not working when the Liberal Government was in office. Every individual Canadian who has the opportunity to work means an improvement is made to the economy. That is what our efforts, consultations and developments of new programs are all about.

The International Year of Youth will give us all an opportunity to rethink the role of young people in our society. Fortunately, Canada's youth is talented, enthusiastic and energetic. Our young people can make a tremendous contribution in all areas of our society.

The ability of our young people to make this contribution depends upon the ability of all Canadians to help them realize their potential and to express themselves in a way that is constructive and beneficial to all of us. Ways must certainly be developed to allow young people to take their rightful place in our society so that they can build productive lives and contribute to the improvement of Canadian life.
During the consultations I have had in the last couple of months I have talked to many young people, and they have told me that they are fed up and disillusioned with the way things have happened in the past. They are looking to us now to develop skills for real, permanent and lasting jobs.
A few months ago, the people of Canada spoke through the electoral process and what they said was that it was time for a change, that it was time for a new and fresh approach to the ills that plague our society. I must say that regardless of how much the Leader of the Opposition wants to encourage us to use the old methods, they simply will not do. When the previous Government was faced with half a million young people out of work, all it could do was to suggest stop-gap measures that did little to relieve the suffering and distress that existed among our young people.
[ Translation]
Since I took up my duties, Mr. Speaker, we have adopted a set of measures to turn the Canadian economy around and enable all Canadians to make a contribution to society through well structured programs.

The motion put before the House today by the Leader of the Opposition is really the kind of approach to the problem that the Canadian people have rejected. It is the idea that if we just go out and throw money at a problem it will go away. How does he expect to solve the problems facing the country when he does not know what they are, and when he has not come to grips with them? How can there be lasting jobs and lasting solutions when that Party's idea of solving issues is to practise confrontational politics?
The Leader of the Opposition talked about First Chance. What he did not talk about was that there was not a single dollar directed to that program.
January 23, 1985
That's a lie.

I have said before that it was an unfunded fantasy. Where were the billion dollars he was talking about? The money was not there.
During the election campaign we told the people of this country that we would again get Canadians working. We have started on that with different programs, some of which are at work at the present time. But we did not use stop-gap measures and we did not make promises of unfunded fantasies. Yes, we have dedicated a billion dollars to job creation and training this year, but we went through the exercise of looking at every program in the expenditures of this Government. We looked at all of them. We reallocated funds. We looked at the priorities which had to be continued. It was a tough exercise to go through, but we ended up with $1 billion dedicated to training, job creation and human resource development in Canada which will provide the jobs, the skills and the security for which Canadians are looking. It will only be a start, because the whole approach which has been taken in the past will have to be turned around. We will not have the short-term, make-work projects that the Liberals liked. We will have the kind of projects that will be ongoing and permanent.
It is because of this, in looking for new approaches and coming up with ways which make skills and training fundamental to our economic development, that I have held consultations across the country with provincial Governments, business, labour, young people, women's groups and native organizations, in order to get their input to the programs which the Government is now considering. I have heard their ideas and I share their concerns. I know what they mean when they say that they do not have opportunities. I hear that all the time. They have not had opportunities in the past. That is what we will address by bringing in a coherent and cohesive policy which will work in all parts of the country and address training and retraining. That means streamlining government programs and eliminating duplications so that public money will be used in the most effective way possible.
The private sector has said: "Yes, we are willing to help in this renewal". We want them to help. The provinces will help. I met with the provinces last week and they indicated that they wanted to co-operate. It is through these consultations that we have discovered there are common themes, concerns and problems which must be addressed by all of us, not only by programs which take in one level of government and ignore the needs and the way in which we can co-operate with people, governments and the private sector in all parts of Canada. We will not use that old unilateralism. That is what the people of Canada rejected on September 4. It is a new spirit of co-operation, confidence and willingness to work together which will make it possible for people to find security.
I noted with interest that the Leader of the Opposition spoke of the need for comprehensive job training and employment opportunity programs. I have to remind him that that is exactly what the previous Government did not give the people

of Canada. There was nothing comprehensive about the ad hoc approach which was taken.

Mr. Speaker, it has been the concern of this Government to turn the situation in this country around, to put Canadians back to work and to give our young people an opportunity to become successfully integrated in our society.

I know that my colleague, the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne), has been addressing this program and consulting in all parts of the country. She spoke eloquently about it the other day. I commend her for the work she has been doing.

We shall be dealing with these problems during the International Year of Youth, but any real and lasting solutions will be the result of concerted and sustained efforts on the part of all groups in our society.

We have announced the formation of new programs and new approaches to deal with this very critical matter, particularly with regard to young people. The steps which we have taken over the past couple of months will lead, through these consultations, to the First Ministers' conference in February and to the economic conference in March. These meetings will provide an opportunity for leading representatives of all parts of the country to chart the future course for Canada.
We face a difficult challenge. It is one which will test the ingenuity and indeed the determination of Canadians everywhere. We must once again get our economy going. We have started to build confidence. We want to ensure that young people have their opportunity in that confident Canada of the future and not the despair that has been left to them. To that end, we have said that within a very short period of time we will be announcing, with the co-operation of the provinces and the private sector, training and job-creation programs for young people this summer. I would remind the Leader of the Opposition once again, although he is somewhat forgetful, that that has been indicated and it will be carried out. I reassure young people everywhere in Canada that that will take place.
I would also remind him that the way in which this Government is approaching job creation, training and skills development is not on an ad hoc basis. We are not saying that the problem can be solved by six-week jobs or ten-week jobs and then throw people back on to unemployment insurance. What we need is a cohesive and coherent approach to this very difficult problem. I can assure the Leader of the Opposition, who has endorsed my training paper today, that we will see that the goals and objectives stated in that paper are put into effect for young people, displaced workers, and the men and women of the country who want nothing more than to be able to find full and satisfying work. That is our commitment to them.

Hear, hear!

The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart).

Mr. Speaker, I must say I was very disappointed with the statement I just heard, made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). I would never have thought that a $40,000 raise could change a person as quickly as it has the Minister. I thought she was one of those Ministers who were compassionate and human and who were there to defend Canadians on middle and low incomes.
I remember when the Minister was in the Opposition: she would ask questions about people in trouble and insist on getting help right away. I remember when the Minister visited my riding with me during the referendum. She was human then, and I would never have thought that an increase in salary would turn the Minister into a defender of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
I do not think Parliament is the appropriate place for putting on an act. It may be for some Members, perhaps, because it is the only thing they can do, but as far as the Minister is concerned, with her personality and her reputation, I cannot understand how she can tell us that the Government has set aside one billion dollars for job creation when she knows perfectly well that the Government has cut four million dollars from programs and projects whose purpose it was to to create jobs. This is money which would otherwise have benefitted Canadian workers.
When the Minister-I am sure her heart is not in it-when the Minister is trying to say that we have the Progressive Conservative Government to thank for the fact that additional jobs have been created, does the Minister also mean it is the Progressive Conservative Government's fault that 1200 jobs are going to be lost at Wabasso and elsewhere? If they want to take credit for the jobs that were created, they will also have to take the blame for the bankruptcies that will occur in this country.
My last question for the Minister .. . This afternoon, I asked specifically if there would be separate Summer Canada budgets for each riding, and the Minister did not answer my question. Does that mean there will be a general budget that will be coordinated, and that disadvantaged ridings like mine and several others will again have to suffer?

Mr. Speaker, I will be making an announcement in due course on that issue. However, I would say to the Hon. Member that I hardly expect-and I am sure he does not-that I will be making that announcement in the House today in response to his question. We as a government
are on a program which will lead us to much more involvement of young people and the development of the objectives of young people in this country. That is set on a schedule which will lead to the best possible development there can be. I can assure the Hon. Member that those programs will be announced very shortly.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to try to put this debate into its proper perspective, just briefly. I do not question the statistics quoted by the Hon. Minister, nor do I question the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) in his address to the House. We all see and hear about these tragic numbers of unemployed youth in our ridings every day. The Leader of the Opposition stated that the 100,000 new jobs created since September 4 are a result of lags in economic policy of six months, 12 months and 18 months and, therefore, should be credited to his Party. I would like to ask the Minister if she feels that the unacceptable numbers of unemployed youth of this country should also be credited to the Liberals as a result of the cumulative effect of poor economic policies by successive Liberal Governments during the last many years?

Mr. Speaker, while there are young people or, for that matter, while there are Canadians unemployed, no one takes any satisfaction. I listened to what the Leader of the Opposition had to say and I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that we can at least hope-and that is what this country is really all about, hope-that the trends of the last few months and the decrease in unemployment among young people continue.
I was looking at the figures and I can say that the unemployment level for young people is down by 56,000 from what it was a year ago. It is down by 29,000 from what it was a month ago. That is a beginning but it is only a beginning. When we look at a total of 500,000, half a million unemployed, we know it is only a beginning. The steps which we are taking, Mr. Speaker, are designed to reduce that number further and continually.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just witnessed the most obvious demonstration of incompetence on the part of a Minister of the Crown, the likes of which I have never seen since I first came to the House.
The Minister gave us a flow of words, or rather a deluge of words which unfortunately fell on a desert of ideas. No specific proposal, Mr. Speaker, nothing at all from a Minister and a government that have already been in office since September. Not a thing! Only accusations against the previous government, a Liberal government which at least had gone to the trouble of creating programs such as Summer Canada. The only obvious thing done by the Minister since taking over her portfolio has been to sack this program which was intended to create tens of thousands of jobs for students this coming summer. That is the only thing she has done, Mr. Speaker.
January 23, 1985

As a result, young people are growing ever more desperate, uncertain as they are already to find jobs next summer.
And now the Minister has just wasted 20 minutes of the time of the House to say absolutely nothing. All Canadians are waiting for the announcements she has been promising all along. As a rule, new programs are announced in December.
I have only one question for the Minister: Whom does she think she is deluding by making such a meaningless speech this afternoon?

Mr. Speaker, once again, I note that a Member of the Liberal Party, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault), is rising to make certain statements and I understand what he is doing this afternoon. However, I can tell him that his concern is more than matched by people on this side of the House. I would also like to remind the Hon. Member just in passing that those comments come from an Hon. Member whose constituency allocation under Canada Works was increased by 66 per cent this year.

Mr. Speaker, I notice that there are some Hon. Members from British Columbia sitting behind the Minister. I hope they had the good grace to be embarrassed when the Minister talked about creating an extra 100,000 jobs in Canada over the last four months, because since the Minister has taken office there has been a net loss of 25,000 jobs in British Columbia. In September there were 1,226,000 people employed in British Columbia. The December statistics which just came out indicate there are 1,201,000 now employed. There are 25,000 jobs less now than there were then.
Perhaps the Minister might want to attribute that to the attitude of the provincial Government under Bill Bennett, as her Leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), had said that he was taking a step in the right direction. Or perhaps she might wish to take credit for that herself.
1 notice that when the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) was in British Columbia last week meeting with a group of young people, she said that young people cannot expect any special preference. She is quoted in an article in the Vancouver Sun on January 19 as saying:
The situation of young people, while deserving special attention, must be examined in the context of the state of society as a whole... A balanced approach must be taken. We can neither neglect nor show favouritism to any particular group.
Would the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) tell us when she is going to do something for the people of British Columbia? When are we going to see some jobs created in B.C. instead of the loss of jobs?

Mr. Speaker, the programs which will be announced very shortly will indeed apply from coast to coast. However, they will take into consideration the regional needs of the country. In the past there have been programs that have come out of Ottawa which were applied in the same way in all parts of the country. That does not work. The example which he has given of British Columbia is a very relevant one.
