Mr. Speaker, I am not especially pleased to find it necessary to rise in support of the motion before the House. With that peculiar kind of naivety which affects new Members I sincerely believed that, despite the philosophical differences between us, the Government would treat the matter of the International Year for Youth with the urgency which the situation of Canada's youth requires. I expected that youth would have an effective spokesperson and that the Government would present bold initiatives consistent with the year's theme of participation, development and peace. Instead we have seen an ideological pursuit of the means of deficit cutting and confidence building based upon the promise of profits for the largely foreign-owned multinationals. At the same time, with unseemly haste, cuts were applied to programs benefiting youth while painful procrastination has yielded only promises of programs to fill the gaps and which will likely benefit profit enterprise more than youth.
The Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) promised to be a spokesperson for youth. I therefore find it rather peculiar that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) responded on behalf of the Government in this debate rather than the Minister of State for Youth. The Minister of State for Youth did promise to be a spokesperson for youth and to express their concerns. Youth are concerned about peace. Where was she when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) became starry-eyed about star wars? Youth are concerned about the environment. Did the Minister extend a helping hand when the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) lay prone before the assault by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on her Ministry? Youth are concerned about controlling their nation's destiny. Where is she as that destiny is being conceded to the economic priorities of foreign profit enterprises?
Canada's youth want to exercise their creative talents. Where was she when thousands of jobs were taken from the cultural community by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse)? Canada's youth are concerned about the Canadiani-zation of our media. Where was she when the CBC was being savaged and as the NFB was rejected in favour of Walt Disney? Canada's youth are concerned about education. What did she say when Summer Canada was cut and 80,000 tuitionearning jobs were destroyed, student loans were frozen and provinces across the land were shutting the doors of our colleges and universities to those who need help most?
Most important, Canada's youth want jobs that will give them a sense of worth and accomplishment that will enhance our society and make it a symbol for all the world of how prosperity can be achieved by a commitment to social justice and peace. Where is she as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Coates) looks to the engines of war as a vehicle for economic growth?

January 23, 1985
Supply
The Minister has intimated that we should place emphasis on what is good about Canadian youth. If she means to praise them for their character and accomplishment, I would join her. However, there is so much happening to them that is wrong. It is wrong that 701,000 young people in this country do not have jobs and that some have never worked and perhaps never will. It is wrong that in some regions such as Newfoundland as much as 70 per cent of the youth are unemployed.
I was in the Atlantic provinces the other day. There is so much there which is wrong. It is wrong that city sidewalks should be crowded with prostituted youths. It is wrong that young people steel food and rob garbage cans in order to eat. It is wrong that soup kitchens and flop houses are the meeting places of jobless and alienated youth. It is wrong that 80 per cent of black youth in Halifax have never been employed. Listen to Father McKenna of Halifax and the voices of St. John's and Sydney. Mr. Speaker, It is tragically wrong when joblessness means hopelessness, a sense of worthlessness, anger and alienation from peers, family and society. Mr. Speaker, it is wrong when old men play with weapons that may not let young people grow old.
It is perhaps unfair to focus upon the Minister of State for Youth for the failure of the Government, for the Government must in its entirety share the blame. However, she is the spokesperson and must impress upon the Government the real meaning of participation, development and peace. It is clear that if one examines the priorities set out by the United Nations to fulfil the requirements of the theme of this year, the Liberal motion must be sustained.
I will delineate in part what those program priorities are. One priority is to increase employment opportunities through formulation of effective programs, policies and plans to reduce unemployment and to eliminate discriminatory employment conditions amont youth. Another priority is to ensure access to every level of education and to make available technical and vocational training, particilarly in rural areas. A third priority is to focus on concerns and the role of young women in development. Yet another is to develop and promote intersectoral community-based activities for health education, sanitation, nutrition, family life education, family planning and other welfare services for youth with the aim of encouraging and facilitating self-care. Another priority is to create an appropriate cultural environment which facilitates the participation of youth in development.
We of the New Democratic Party have made positive proposals in respect to youth. In urging the Minister and the Government to fulfil their promise to the young people of Canada we have several recommendations for their consideration and implementation. We recommend the allocation of $1 billion to a youth initiative fund to allow young people to create their own jobs. We recommend an industrial grant levy system to provide training opportunities for young people. We recommend the restoration of the 6 and 5 per cent cuts imposed by the former Government to post-secondary education and additional funding to ensure quality, relevance and access and assured levels of funding in colleges and universities. We recommend a House standing committee on youth in order that all Parties may be involved in determining what the priorities should be with respect to this year. A national advisory council on post-secondary education should also be considered in connection with steps to ensure accessibility to the university system.
More than this and those five regional fora that have been described by the Minister, let her ensure that the youth are listened to and heeded on all the important issues of the day rather than just those affecting youth. They should be listened to on the issues of peace, the environment, our Canadian culture, economic development, equality between the sexes for all people, employment, disarmament, peace and so on.
Finally, let the Government change from bashing the deficit, and therefore the poor, to the creation of jobs as a first priority. The New Democratic Party has been clear on what initiatives should be taken and I commend those initiatives to the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to put a question to the Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy). As members will know, the Government has eliminated Summer Canada which is a program specifically designed to provide employment primarily to students during the summer months to give them the opportunity to earn so that they may continue their studies in the fall. That may not be such a problem in cities like Toronto or Montreal where the unemployment rate may be very low. However, in single industry communities, of which there are 811 across the country, it is extremely important for that kind of program to be put into effect because they do not have the corporate base on which to employ people.
What is his view with respect to ensuring that there be early notice and announcement of such a program specifically designed for summer employment for young people?

Mr. Speaker, I have been quite willing to attribute the most sincere and constructive intention on the part of the Minister of Employment and Immigration with respect to the introduction of summer employment programs for youth. However, in my view, it is the height of irresponsibility to accede to cuts in Summer Canada without having something to replace that program. It has caused a great deal of uncertainty and insecurity among young people and for many it is already too late to make decisions with respect to the coming year.
There is another aspect of Summer Canada which has been discovered in our consultations on the East Coast and elsewhere through communications received in many of our offices. It is that Summer Canada presented an opportunity to provide services to the disabled, for example, as well as others in our society who needed social services of some kind which were provided by young people. Not only have young people been deprived of the opportunity to earn money for tuition and other expenses, but a number of valuable services which are being extended to people in difficulty in our society have been
January 23, 1985

placed in jeopardy and are uncertain. That is also a serious matter.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) indicated in her remarks that she entered into consultations with a number of groups in the country on employment programs. Of course, we welcome and applaud that action. However, she neglected to mention one group which tends to be forgotten by policy formulators, the disabled who constitute some 10 per cent of the total Canadian population. Within that group there is an unemployment rate of up to 80 per cent, such as the blind population where the unemployment rate is probably in excess of 80 per cent.
Prior to the election the Conservatives indicated to at least one of the major organizations, COPOH, that they would be willing to consider introducing a program of contract compliance within the recommendations that have been made by the House of Commons Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. In his considerations for this debate, has my colleague given any thought at all to programs that would go a long way to helping the disabled become fully participating members in the mainstream of Canadian life?

Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fact, we had occasion to talk to representatives of the organizations providing care for and composed of the disabled. I believe the Government should implement compulsory contract compliance which is a measure that group has been seeking. In that respect I would note that on August 14, 1984 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said with respect to whether compulsory contract compliance should be provided: "Yes, along the lines proposed in recommendations 26 and 27 of the 1981 Obstacles Report".

Mr. Speaker, could the Hon. Member clarify the extent to which he believes contract compliance should go? Should it go to the smallest of businesses in Canadian society or should it apply only to big business?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that most of those who have an understanding of contract compliance as it has been implemented in other jurisdictions and been considered appropriate for implementation generally accord some limit of numbers of employees below which it would not be compulsory. I think that is something that would have to be taken into account with respect to deliberations and consultations on such legislation when it is brought forward.
Mr.Speaker, could we have an idea of the NDP policy with respect to those limits?
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest 100 employees.
Further questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to participate in this debate and I believe it is most significant that the Liberal Party has chosen to address the Government's responsibility for youth on this our first Opposition day of the New Year. As this House reopens, we mark the beginning of International Youth Year, a year
Supply
during which attention will be focused on recognizing and meeting the needs of our young people.
The Tories won the confidence of the population and were elected to effect change. They promised our youth a rose garden but to date, all they have delivered is a thorny bush. I have already said on a number of occasions in the House that the situation in which the youth of this country find themselves is tragic.
Many councils, much research and numerous studies have produced reports identifying the specific concerns and have provided the Government with the starting points for legislative action. A two-year in-depth study by Professor Reginald Bibby, Professor of Sociology at the University of Lethbridge, based on a survey of 3,530 teenagers was published in the Ottawa Citizen on January 21. It states that adolescents have pointed out that adults are against them. I find that very sad. They feel that their opinions do not matter and that they are powerless.
Indeed, both the action and the inaction of the present Government seems to substantiate the thought, feelings and claims of our youth. The teenagers are saying that they must manifest their own values and work hard as young people to emerge as whole individuals.
High on the young people's list of interests and concerns are unemployment, friendship circles, cultural events, sexuality, child abuse and crime, nuclear war, drugs and suicide. These reports lead one to believe that the Government should be directing activity toward supporting any projects or proposals aimed at these particularly crucial issues.
Let us look at the economic perspective of what the Government has done to see the situation today. The major area of youth concern has been that of jobs and the opportunity to feel that they can be active participants with a worth-while role and place in society. With no government programs or policies in place, their sense of deception is profound and it can affect them and society fundamentally in the future.
The elimination of the First Chance program by the Conservatives is perhaps the most blatant indication of lack of care and concern toward our young people's needs. This program was the most important public policy set forward by government in the interests of youth since Prime Minister St. Laurent established the responsibility and role of the federal government for support to secondary education. Prior to establishing this First Chance program concept-and as the Conservatives have this incredible penchant for only consultation and no action, perhaps this will be of interest to their Members- major consultations were held with the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Chamber of Commerce, the Business Council on National Issues, and the provinces. The reasoning which was discussed was very sound and very important. While the Government was spending billions of dollars, in fact $4 to $5 billion on postsecondary education, these programs were targeted to a small percentage of our youth who continue on to college and university. Very little was being done for the three-quarters of

January 23, 1985
Supply
our youth population who did not continue on to post-secondary education. Very few dollars are being directed toward their preparation and training. This was key. First Chance was a fair initiative by the federal Government to meet their needs. The cut from $100 million to $27 million in the youth training option, the First Chance type of program to serve only three to four thousand youth instead of the anticipated 10,000, and the cut of the $1 billion proposed and committed to serve 100,000 for this next fiscal exercise is inexcusable. It is poor planning and it shows a tremendous lack of caring. This is where the major area of unemployment problems are found. This is where unemployment is highest and this is where we need to put our effort.
Scaling down First Chance to an experimental program, cutting back funding to $27 million when the value and the need for this program is so evident and there is a necessity to go full steam ahead is unacceptable. In addition to the fact that no replacement project of acceptable proportion has been put in place, it surprises me that it was cut. It meets all the criteria for the True Blue. First Chance served the interests of the private sector as well as our youth. The programs were designed and tailored to the training needs of local and regional industry. The employer had his extra costs met as well as having a first crack at trained employees and could then keep permanently those who demonstrated high motivation. The employer serves as a good corporate citizen, the new entrant employee's First Chance salary was paid by the federal government.
The new entrant, during this transition from school to the work force acquires self-confidence, skills, good work habits and a sense of personal worth, in other words, a chance to earn and learn. That is what you cut out, a chance to earn and learn.
This First Chance program was a training program not a job creation one. It received support from the private sector and focused on those in difficulty. It was a co-operative program between government, the private sector, and community groups.

Young people have casual or temporary jobs for short periods which provide no security and force them to make only short-term plans. For our young people, unemployment is more than just statistical economic data; it is a factual reality, and for many of them, it jeopardizes their chances at independence. It means constant insecurity, the absence of autonomy, the impossibility of making long-term personal plans, and even more serious for both, society and young people themselves, it means a loss of value of their theoretical training if it cannot be put in practice soon enough. When there is no great demand for a particular field of training, employers prefer experience and they have a lot of choice. Many workers then enter a vicious circle: no experience means no job, and no job
means no experience. Part-time employment is also a form of hidden unemployment with which many must be satisfied. [English]
The youth unemployment level is almost twice that of the national level. By not taking action now, the Government risks establishing life-long negative attitudes of our young toward society because it is creating, through economic inaction, a generation of frustrated, discouraged, and therefore unproductive citizens. Unemployment of our visible minority youth is over 85 per cent. Handicapped and native youth need special consideration in employment. Employment equity as outlined in the Abella report is worthy of very careful consideration, and then mandatory affirmative action is needed. It is not only needed, but it is a moral imperative.
This is not just short-term disillusionment that we are looking at, it is a tragedy. Our youth need work and appropriate training. These are the key issues.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, it is a well established fact that the higher education one has, the easier it is to find a job. The situation is this: Of the great many young people who enter our education system, very few graduate with a terminal degree. And even among those graduating with a terminal degree, many cannot find a job. That is why we need special training programs which would ease the transition from the school to the labour market. This challenge could improve the training and maximize job opportunities.
The government, on the one hand, encourages young people to continue their education, while, on the other hand, the Bovey Commission suggests that tuition fees should be increased and student loans have been frozen. Some encouragement!

From the cultural perspective, what do we see? Cuts to the CBC children's unit, cuts to the Canada Council, cuts to the National Film Board, governmental agencies that are supposed to protect and reflect who we are, proud Canadians. "Oh, Canada, we stand on guard for thee" does not seem to be the Tory anthem. I put you on guard. It is our anthem, and we expect you to respect that.
How does the Government feel about the high proportion of non-Canadian programming currently available to our young people? Does it not realize that we as Canadians have ideas and creativity to offer in the area of culture? Should we not be promoting our Canadian identity, instilling a sense of pride in our youth in their distinctiveness? Would the Minister not have a feeling of accomplishment in the various Ministries that have supported policies to encourage Canadian initiatives?
The reduction of more than $75 million from the CBC budget, $3.5 million from the National Film Board, to mention but a few cases, reflects a major prejudice against both the cultural development and the economy of Canada. It is also a negation of the importance of a distinctive Canadian culture and our future generations will suffer the consequences.
January 23, 1985

According to Statistics Canada, 414,000 people are employed in work related to the arts, either within cultural organizations or as individual artistic creators. This level of employment is nearly equivalent to that involved in agricultural production in Canada or to the number employed in the federal civil service.
One of the immediate consequences of these budgetary cut-backs in the cultural industries is the reduction of employment, with concomitant negative effects on the economy, and certainly on our identity. Contrary to this spirit of Canadian direction, which we even see in the Investment Canada Act but do not know how it is defined, the Government remained passive while the CRTC refused consideration of an application by the National Film Board for its Young Canada Television/Telejeunesse Canada. Here was an innovative proposal for French and English service, directly aimed at filling gaps in existing broadcasting. This youth-oriented cable channel offered high Canadian content and comprehensively included programming for children and youths aged 2 to 17. [Translation]
The National Film Board's proposal was not the only one. There were others, but none offered such a comprehensive range of options capable of directly addressing young people and reflecting our cultural and national identity. As a matter of fact, the Canadian content of the other proposals was only 25 per cent. As to the rest, they were programs originating from England or the United States, depicting the American way of life, and not concentrating on issues young Canadians are confronted with. These things which make us different.
With respect to according this private youth-oriented cable channel, the NFB proposition would have included young people. In addition it would have given them the capacity to "help themselves", to use the Minister's phrase, and funding would have come from private industry, lotteries and subscriber fees. Government funding would have been in the form of a loan. The Board was not asking for hand-outs or free money.
The NFB proposal seemed to meet every criterion laid out by the Tory Government when talking of job creation and youth-oriented programming. It relied on private sector input. It directly involved young people. It responded to an identifiable lack in existing programs and addressed social and health issues which have not yet been effectively examined.
However, the National Film Board was caught in a classic catch-22 orchestrated by the CRTC in which the Government neglected to intervene-no approval, no licence; no licence, no authorization to approach the private sector for necessary funds. Yesterday I expressed my displeasure at attacks on the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne). I meant that quite sincerely. She is not the person; it is the role and the mandate which she fills that I attack. I hope she understands that. Today I must ask her once again to define her commitment in her role to our young people.
Supply
In replying to pointed questions from my confreres, the Minister conveniently shifted responsibility to her fellow Ministers. This passing of the buck is unacceptable. The Minister of State for Youth should realize that her colleagues have not been acting in the interests of youth, nor have they intervened on behalf of young people. Youth need her support. They need her advocacy. They want to hear her speaking out loud; they cannot hear her in caucus. Where has her voice been? For example, in terms of the National Film Board proposal, did she contact the CRTC? Did she speak with the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse)? Those are the kinds of things which we are hoping the Minister will be able to accomplish.
An opportunity to focus effectively and innovatively on youth concerns has slipped through the Government's hands. I am sure that is not what she wanted, or I hope it was not what she wanted. Its inaction has bitterly disappointed members of youth councils Canada-wide, as well as young Canadians and their parents.
I could elaborate further on the crucial implication of the Government's inaction with respect to the issue of youth broadcasting policies and programming. What is so astounding and distressing is that this is but one area in a list of many where youth concerns are being neglected, blatantly neglected. The Government has been eager to cut not one but a dozen programs and budgets aimed at helping our youth in the areas of employment, education, training and development. It seems to me that the Government has put dollars before humans. The Government continues to make a mockery of the themes of participation, development and peace.
From the social perspective, what has the Tory Government done? Program after program has been stripped by the Tory Government. Katimavik, for example, is a national youth service aimed at helping in the personal development of its participants and providing opportunities for a greater understanding of the country.

Young Quebeckers were very fond of the Katimavik program. I hope that the Minister is aware of that.

In the past two years, over 8,500 young people have taken part in this exciting venture. They have learned and lived what is Canada. Recently, however, more than $20 million was cut from the Katimavik budget. I ask why. Why cut a program which was specifically geared toward the themes of participation, development and peace?
Sadly, the list goes on. The Young Worker's Exchange Program was also eliminated. This program offered the means by which young Canadians could gain a better understanding of themselves, of society and of other countries. Their discoveries helped them in their development as individuals and in their ability to make further contributions to Canada. We should be looking ahead to the future of our country. We should be training our youth to be proud and to appreciate being Canadian and knowing what is going on in the rest of the world. Youth represent our most precious human asset and

January 23, 1985
Supply
resource. We cannot afford to let them drift aimlessly. We are taking away from them opportunities to develop independence and responsibility. We cannot do that.
Social housing and co-op cuts are of concern. For the growing number of single parent families with low incomes, shelter and a decent place to live with their families is absolutely vital. I wonder if the Minister is aware of the growing suicide rate among young people. I find it very difficult to absorb the statistics and their implications.
[ Translation]
The suicide rate has increased by 400 per cent since the seventies. Even if I quote statistics for Quebec, the situation is similar elsewhere in Canada. Every week, eight young Quebeckers commit suicide and for each one who succeeds, 100 fail. This is serious.
Road accidents are the main cause of those deaths but some experts believe that many drownings, hunting and road accidents are really suicide attempts. Some young Canadians have told us about their fears, their despair and their doubts. Moreover, we are told that if we do not listen to them, the suicide rate will increase.

The questions of sexual exploitation of the young through the use of juveniles in pornography and prostitution and the high incidence of child abuse reported by the Badgley Commission are looming. Where does the Minister of State for Youth stand on these crucial issues? Will she begin to make herself heard, to act as the interlocutor for young people? Will she begin to oppose actions which greatly reduce and threaten opportunity for our young people? Will she appear at any hearings which involve the concerns of our young people?
The Minister of State for Youth stated yesterday that she would soon be putting into place an information and communication committee to listen to the concerns of young people. I wonder why, almost one month after the beginning of International Year of Youth and five months after the beginning of this Government, this committee was not in place at the outset of 1985. Moreover, I wonder why programs were cut before this committee was consulted. Existing programs should have at least been left in place until new Tory initiatives are ready to go. No wonder the youth of this country are discouraged and disoriented. The Government seems to be working in reverse-cut then consult, act and pick up the pieces later.
Can the Minister give the House and, more important, the youth of the country, some reassurance and a commitment on her part to become a true advocate? This winter has been particularly bitter for young Canadians. It saddens me to realize that it will only get colder if the Tory Government does not start to act in their interests, in the interests of all Canadian families.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) spoke, he stated that 36 per cent of all unemployed are between the ages 18 and 24. He went on to say that a time lag of six, twelve and even eighteen months exists before government policy decisions begin to show up. Does the Hon. Member agree with her Leader that the current high levels of youth unemployment are the disastrous results of Liberal Government policies?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I sometimes wonder if the Member recognizes that he lives in a very privileged country which had policies in place that supported an incredible international recession. This international recession was not suffered to the same degree in Canada as it was in the rest of the world because we had a wonderful security net in place. The fact that that safety net may have cost some money and increased the deficit is not what requires extra concern at this particular moment. What is important is that our youth and their families were supported.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member on her speech. I am glad she mentioned the hiring criteria of the federal Government. I want to observe for the benefit of the House that the problem is more serious this year than ever before because this Government has done away with the direct employment programs for youth like Environment 2000. There is no such program. It has taken the hiring criteria left over from the federal-provincial agreement on need.
I want to mention briefly to the House the case of a widow living at home on a pension from CN of $350 a month. She has two sons aged 18 and 19 who are at home. They have finished school and cannot find work. She has a daughter who came out of trade school with a bookkeeping course. There is a federal job creation program in that community, but not one of them qualified for. a referral under a job creation program. Welfare does not pay for children after they reach the age of 18. Even though the daughter was trained in the trade school and the two sons are capable of working, not one of them qualified for a referral under a job creation program in that community.
The community wants to hire somebody from that family, but it is not allowed to do so. Why? Because the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) signed the hiring regulations which state that first they have to take someone who is on social assistance. The social assistance may be higher than what could be made on the program because Canada Works pays only $200 a week. They then have to take people on UIC even though somebody may be getting the maximum $255 a week on UIC. Forcing that person to go to work for $200 a week will take food out of the mouths of his children.
I have a question to ask. Does the Hon. Member not feel that this is absolute, plain discrimination against the youth of

this country and against unemployed mothers who are seeking work? Is it not disgraceful that the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) has not been successful in convincing the Minister of Employment and Immigration to change the hiring criteria after cutting off the direct job creation programs for youth?

Mr. Speaker, I will begin with a brief comment. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) mentioned the suicide statics, which are of concern to all of us.
I brought those statistics to the attention of her predecessor in 1980 in the form of a prediction of a logical consequence of the policy initiatives being put in place at that time, including the National Energy Program and other policy initiatives. I brought that to the attention of the former Prime Minister. I said that if those policies were followed, suicide rates would go up. It gives me no pleasure to have her confirm that that advice was not taken and that the consequences did follow.
The Hon. Member raised the matter of employment in the cultural industries and brought to the attention of the House that over 400,000 people are currently employed in those industries. Having come to the House with that kind of figure, I would assume that she has done her homework. Can she enlighten the House as to what portion of those jobs are totally government supported and what portion are private sector supported?
Can she also indicate how many of those jobs disappeared in the last four years because of economic policy which made it impossible for people to buy tickets, books or records? Is it not clear to her that the 1983-84 report of Employment and Immigration showed that 37,200 jobs had been created by all of these marvellous programs for the youth of this country, person years of employment, and that this new Government in four months has created over 50,000 jobs for young people? Will she admit that maybe we are on the right track and that it is better for the cultural industries and better for youth to follow the course that this Government was elected to follow?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief comment. I have listened to the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and previous Ministers of Employment and Immigration. To tell you the truth, there is not much difference. I hear the same sort of promises, studies, how things will get better and how we are following the right economic course. Of course, nothing got any better for young people in the last number of years.
To hear the Liberals now blame it all on the Tories who have been in power for four months is somewhat hypocritical. They have to accept a fair amount of the blame for the state in which young people find themselves today.
Liberals quote figures about suicides among young people. A year and a half ago I rose in this House to make a statement about a young artist in my constituency who had been on unemployment insurance. Attempting to do something about his state, he started a small company which made posters so that young people learning to play the guitar could look at a poster rather than a book. The unemployment insurance scheme decreed that he was self-employed and cut off all benefits. The man was without any resources and ended up killing himself. That was laid on the doorstep of the Liberal regime and all of their little niggly type of regulations they had introduced into the UIC scheme.
The Conservatives came to power on promises of reform and new hope for young people. Young people in this country are thoroughly disappointed because there is no new hope from this bunch. In fact, it is just a continuation. It is blaming the victim, blaming the young, and blaming the unemployed. They are the ones who are shouldering all of the hardships in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday and again today, a number of Members of the Official Opposition, showed, more or less appropriately, their affinity for culture and drama. I know one role that would fit them like a glove, and that is the role of Tartuffe, the impostor.
How can a Party that has dashed the hopes and aspirations of an entire generation of young Canadians tell us what to do? We have been in power for only four months, while they held the reins for almost 22 years without interruption. They would have us believe that they would have been able to achieve in four months what they were unable to accomplish in 22 years. Who knows-hindsight is a wonderful thing.
The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) said that between 16 and 37 per cent of our young people are unemployed, and I say that is an immediate consequence of her Party's policies when it was in power. These policies have led to an alarming increase in the unemployment rate among
the young. Now the Liberals have the unmitigated gall to hold us responsible for this situation today.
In June 1984, the number of young Canadians who had jobs dropped by 278,000 compared to March 1980, which is when the Liberals came back to power. Between 1980 and 1983, the youth unemployment rate rose from 13.2 to 19.9 per cent in the country as a whole. The number of young people without full-time employment rose by 406,000 between 1980 and 1983. In 1983, the number of young people with jobs dropped by 97,000 in Quebec and 80,000 in Ontario compared to 1980. And now we are being accused of failing to correct the situation in four months!
The Liberal Government's training programs were inadequate and were not set up in terms of labour market requirements.
Programs designed specifically to alleviate youth unemployment were short-term projects only and were not sufficiently geared to the training or job experience already acquired by participants. Although the situation was serious, the Liberals made very few attempts to coordinate their activities with those of the provinces, municipalities and the private sector or to make their programs compatible with long-term economic development programs in various regions.
I said the other day in the House that as we embark full of hope on this International Year of Youth, we must bear in mind that our aim is not to find some magic formula. Neither should it be to encourage hypocrisy. With nearly one-half million unemployed young people on its conscience, the Official Opposition wants to set itself up as an arbiter ... Let us not be obscene!
What kind of credibility can we assign to the Liberal Party's recriminations and tales of woe? What kind of credibility does a political party deserve which sees Canadian youth as shiftless, suicidal, alcoholic, addicted to drugs and delinquent? This deliberately pessimistic view is an insult to our young people and to anyone's intelligence. Fortunately, most young Canadians are sound in mind and in body. They are diligent and active, with a thirst, yes, but a thirst for life and for ideals.
According to the results of a poll published this week to which the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) was referring earlier, young Canadians care most about friendship. Is it friendship to say that they are just a bunch of failures? Friendship means helping people to stand on their two feet.
I certainly do not mean that this Government intends to leave disadvantaged youth to its own devices, but I think it is rather far-fetched to see this group as representative of Canadian youth, as a whole.
So if you please, stop shedding those crocodile tears, as I asked you earlier this week. Stop using youth for political gains. I ask you once more, please! The interests of the young are at stake.
As Jean-Paul Sartre once said: "The essential thing is not what has been done with Man, but what Man does with what
January 23, 1985

has been done with him." In a political environment, reflecting on that thought can be most comforting. It is indeed when, for instance, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) gives me but two alternatives: either, as she says, I do not understand the nature of my mandate, or my colleagues do not listen to me. I put it to the Hon. Member that I have a very clear notion of what my mandate is, and I am in a better position than she is to assess the impact I have on my colleagues.
For the past four months, the Government to which I am privileged to belong, has been working actively. And soon, very soon my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) will show how unfair such criticism by the Opposition is with respect to youth training and employment. What is to be announced will have nothing in common with the previous Government's huge but unrealistic, if not unworkable, training program. It would take a serious dose of bad faith to shed tears over programs that have been altered or simply cancelled because they were failures, without waiting for the new programs to be announced very soon.
Also, I am working in close co-operation with my colleagues whose responsibilities partly concern our youth. However, it would be premature to report on our exchanges here. All the areas, all the issues referred to by my counterparts from the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party are part of our concerns. Rome was not built in one day.
Contrary to what the Opposition is suggesting, the International Youth Year in Canada was launched under the best of auspices.
When travelling across our great country, I have been able to see that the International Youth Year everywhere is being met with the same enthusiasm. It is being supported equally by the young, the various levels of Government, the business community, labour and non-governmental organizations.
Last Monday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, and she has repeated it today, that Liberal Members stubbornly refuse to see anything positive in this Government's doings. Given such blindness, I think it is appropriate to say that, like my Cabinet colleagues and contrary to the practices of the previous government, I had very fruitful discussions with my provincial counterparts in November and December. Indeed, we have agreed to keep in touch and the same thing goes for our other social partners.
Having stressed that International Youth Year is more than a program and a series of projects, having emphasized that it will be a year to reflect and take action, I should like to explain the program envisaged by the Canadian government to mark the occasion.
Before mentioning specific projects already approved and to show our openmindedness, let me define the context within which we in the government make such grants.
First of all, we want to encourage young people to carry out various projects which will open their mind to their personal and collective situation, and to give us their advice on the best way to find long-term solutions to their problems.
Supply
We do not think that young people can do everything themselves. That is why I decided that eligibility criteria for grants should include a salary or a fee which, among other things, will make it possible for young applicants to use the services of advisers who will help them draft their bids and administer their projects. That will give them an opportunity to benefit from the experience of their elders.
We do not intend to reject any worthwhile project sponsored by young people simply because it would require financing to see it through. I hasten to point out that I do not claim exclusive rights over that initiative since it was recommended to me by groups of young people whose projects had been cavalierly turned down by the previous administration.
Unlike our predecessors, we in this government will go out of our way to ensure that young people have ready access to any program offered to them. Instead of saying simply the program is there, just use it, we tell them how they should proceed to take full advantage of it.
The way we operate is to personalize programs for young people so that they will know where they stand without worrying about red tape.
To promote the implementation of special projects undertaken by or for young people through voluntary groups and organizations, we have allocated over $1 million in grants in recent months.
Let me give a few examples of the subsidies we have granted.
To the National YMCA Council, we have allocated $94,500 to organize, for young people between the ages of 18 and 25, a leadership development program which will include local, national and international studies.
To the organizing committee of the 32th World Congress of the International Federation of Youth and Music, we have granted $50,000 to finance a series of seven regional concerts to be held throughout the country in which will take part 500 young musicians of the 37 member countries of the Federation.
To the Societe de recherche en orientation humaine Inc., we have granted $20,000 to organize an international seminar in Montreal.
To the Last Touch Regional Youth Council Inc., we have allocated $75,000 for a national conference organized by young people from Saskatchewan to be held in Fort San next August.
The Conference on Young People and the Law has also received a grant to bring together at an international conference young lawyers and para-legal workers as well as law students. The conference will be held in Montreal in 1985.
A subsidy will help a youth committee to organize the winter games for native youths to be held in Winnipeg during the week beginning February 17. The games are open to all native youths in Manitoba and will include various sports.

January 23, 1985

An amount of $5,000 has been allocated to the Canadian Ecumennical Youth Coalition to organize a national consultation of young people within the framework of the triennial assembly of the Canadian Council of Churches to be held in Halifax. Its purpose will be to promote increased participation by young people in the decision-making process of Churches.
These are but a few examples. We are not giving our grants in an haphazard fashion, but on the contrary for a precise objective: obtaining from our young people their views on issues which are important to them, their current development and future orientation.
I have stated many times that our action is based on consultation and concertation. The previous government might claim that so was its own action. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you something. During my initial round of consultations which I held with my provincial counterparts responsible for the International Year of Youth, three of them emphasized that they had had more contacts over the past three months with federal ministers about programs of common interest than during the last five years of the Liberal administration. Imagine that!
This is not much, really, compared with the problems and difficulties of all kinds that members of the Official Opposition left at our door on September 4. So, whatever our efforts, they will certainly be more positive that those of the previous government. Which does not mean that we will be satisfied with doing the minimum, or that we will do just about anything.

Mr. Speaker, young people are very concerned about the quality of university education. I agree with the Minister wholeheartedly that many of the problems which young people face certainly did not originate in the last four months. Those problems have originated because of past policies of former Liberal Governments.
One of their sins was the radical change in the cost-sharing arrangements between the provinces and the federal Government respecting higher education. I felt-and certainly my colleagues in the NDP felt-that transferring money in an unrestricted way contributed to the decrease in funding by the provinces toward higher education. Today we are finding that many students across the country are being turned away because facilities, teaching staff and classroom space are inadequate. More and more universities are restricting the numbers of students who are able to enter the system, either by increasing the academic standards or by increasing tuition. The latter is the most repugnant, because it means that only the sons and daughters from well-to-do families will be able to afford education, and the universality of the higher education system will soon erode.
I wonder if the Minister would care to comment on the very important area of the financing of higher education, and
indicate whether she has made suggestions to her Cabinet colleagues, particularly the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) who is responsible for funding and federal contributions to the provinces. In addition, could she indicate if she has met with the National Union of Students to hear their concerns about funding for higher education?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am quite concerned about that problem. We have held discussions with the Secretary of State, and the problem is on the agenda for our next meeting with the Secretary of State. He has just returned from a meeting with the provinces in which this was the main subject of conversation. We have not yet had the time for a report, but I expect it very soon. I am sure the Minister will be glad to answer that question more precisely in a few days.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have had some consultations with officials of the Minister's Department and have concluded that one of the priorities for spending in the coming year relates to the funding of cultural activities for young people, in particular those who might become performing artists in groups like Jeunesse Musicale. An I correct in drawing the conclusion that one of the priorities for spending in the International Year for Youth is for cultural organizations?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would be mistaken in saying that it is a priority, even though it might be within my heart to want to make it a priority. I think that to help the Jeunesse Musicale in the middle of an international conference is very important, but I have enumerated quite a number of the grants, some of which are related to the cultural field. There is not really one sector which is placed over another. It depends on the projects which are presented. The recommendations which come from the Department depend on the project itself, and not necessarily on the field to which it relates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the comments of the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne). She spoke about young people who are excellent and exemplary citizens who will undoubtedly be more effective than we are, but the Minister should admit just the same that there is also a large number of young people in trouble.
I think that all members of all parties in this House would rather have no unemployment at all. We all agree on that.
However, should we not be a little more realistic and humane? Being from Quebec as myself, do you not think that there are thousands of young Quebecers who are experiencing discrimination as far as social welfare is concerned? Young people receive only $150 a month. Until the private sector is reorganized and a full employment policy is implemented, would it not be advisable, rather than let them starve, to provide short-term projects to enable them to work or get some
January 23, 1985

new training? I feel that there is an element of compassion in those projects.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne). When she met her provincial counterparts, did she ask the minister responsible in Quebec to alter his discriminatory policy with respect to young Quebeckers, whose social welfare benefits are reduced by 50 per cent solely because they are under 30 years of age?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, like my hon. colleague I would be most happy if we could completely stamp out unemployment, discard this word once and for all in Canada. But this will not happen overnight, and as was said earlier, we have met with problems. He has referred to the short-term, to retraining. We have seen how the Liberal Government's short-term policies worked out. As a result, the situation has but worsened. This is why this Government, as the Minister so aptly suggested earlier, would like to substitute to the short term something that has a better chance of enduring. As regards retraining, please be a little patient. The Minister told you earlier that she would be announcing whatever plans she has, and 1 am not here to speak for her.
You were wondering whether I was aware that many people have trouble finding jobs and do not qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. I could tell you about the situation of people you may not even be aware of yourself. I could tell you about the artists, since you are constantly bringing that up, who can never qualify for those benefits. I could tell you about film technicians who never have an opportunity to work 20 weeks in a row. What have you ever done about that?
I remember very well representations that were made to the previous Government on that matter. They were laughed away. I would therefore think that before blaming me after four months, one should look further back and not assume that I am unaware of the issues.
Concerning the problems you referred to with respect to the Quebec Minister, I would point out to you that the Minister whom I have met the most frequently is the one who is responsible for the International Youth Year and President of the Treasury Board. He is not responsible for the problems you referred to.

Mr. Speaker, I find some of the comments made by the Minister to be a bit grandiose and hypocritical in the sense that she seems to be operating in a vacuum. May I forewarn her and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) that there are other Ministries of the Government which have a direct effect on the creation of jobs in Canada. Far be it for me, Mr. Speaker, to remind the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration of one such agency, namely the CBC, and the cut-backs which have occurred there, with the accompanying loss of jobs not only for

employees, technicians and artists, but for other individuals who have had contract work with the CBC. Therefore, I cannot understand the Minister's thinking. Can she confirm to the House whether, in fact she is the lead Minister of this Government in setting forth a strategy for youth employment in Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in this Government, Sir, there is a Minister of Employment. This Minister is not myself. I am the spokesperson for youth. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted with this opportunity to take part in the debate today, first of all as the former Minister of State for Youth and second, because my Leader has proposed a motion today to draw the attention of the House to that very important subject, our young people. This issue was raised in the House thanks to the Official Opposition. Since Parliament reconvened and in fact since we started a new session, this Government has failed to take any time in the House to propose measures that will benefit our youth. It was therefore up to the Opposition to raise this issue and to discuss the concerns and problems of young Canadians. Canada's future and prosperity is in the hands of our young people, and the federal Government therefore has a duty to ensure that young Canadians are equipped to undertake the task of sustaining Canada's growth.
The creation of a special portfolio for youth almost a year ago was the Liberal Government's way of showing that it was aware of the problems besetting Canada's youth and that it would give young people its special attention.
1 was listening to the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) criticize the former Government. I would say she has us to thank for the youth portfolio and her seat in Cabinet, since the portfolio was created by the Liberal Government.
But I should like to examine now what has become of the portfolio of the Minister of State for Youth under this Progressive Conservative government. When the debate was opened earlier this afternoon, we saw the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDonald) "shove aside" the Minister of State for Youth, make her remarks and give the news she could. The Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) took a back-seat to her, and the government has demonstrated

January 23, 1985
Supply
through its actions that she is just a junior minister not only in the House, but in all government decisions.
Under the Liberal government, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Youth never played second fiddle to his colleagues. He had his own responsibilities. This Minister has allowed the Ministry of State for Youth to become the puppet of Employment and Immigration. Now, she has no choice but to kowtow to the Minister of Employment and Immigration to exert some influence with regard to youth employment policies. She has given up on the Student Exchange Program. Under Liberal governments, the Minister of State for Youth was responsible for Student Exchange Programs. Again, this Minister must bow and scrape to her colleagues.
As far as employment programs are concerned, she calmly accepted the cancellation of Summer Canada. She let this program be completely destroyed, Mr. Speaker. Now, the Minister of State for Youth must make empty speeches such as the one we heard today. I am not blaming the Minister, but I do blame her Government, which is leaving her with the simple job of taking care of public relations for the International Youth Year. She has no other responsibility or power in the Government.
This shows how low a priority the new Progressive Conservative Government is giving to the situation of young people.
I want to remind the Minister that her role is to speak on behalf of young people in Cabinet, not the opposite, Mr. Speaker. What she is doing today is to sing the praises of her Government without worrying about the problems of young people. In my opinion, this is not consistent with the mandate she received as Minister of State for Youth. She has now become a spokesperson for big business and the banking friends of the Progressive Conservative Party, and the only issue which does not concern her is the situation of young people. Yet, her mandate is quite clear. It is not to be the Government public relations officer for young people, but rather to be the soul and conscience of the Government where young people are concerned.
Mr. Speaker, what has the Minister done in the last five months? What has she announced? She has spoken only of consultations, and conference after circumference as one of your political heroes would have said. I think that the only speech I heard the Minister of State for Youth make which was reported in the newspapers is the one where she said: "As Minister of State for Youth, I shall take care of those who are doing well." However, I wish to remind the Minister that those who are doing well do not need her. Those who need the support of a politician like herself are those who are having problems in our society.
I wish the Minister of State for Youth would stop turning a blind eye to those of our young people who are not as successful and that she would realize that as the Minister, she is
politically and socially responsible for providing equal opportunities for all elements of our society.
Since proportionally, more young Canadians are unemployed than any other group of Canadians, action is necessary to correct this situation.
We have been treated to a flood of words from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), but she has yet to make an announcement today. She says she will be making one soon, and it is high time, Mr. Speaker, because we are nearing the end of January. Usually, students could count on programs being announced before the holidays so they could prepare projects and proposals. Companies accustomed to hiring students would know about the programs and be able to plan their activities for the summer, while now, it seems- yes, she said very shortly she would be announcing programs, but her announcement will come at a time when students are starting to prepare for their exams. And, of course, there is the approval process and the usual red tape. When will students be sure they will have a summer job, Mr. Speaker? That is what worries us.
I realize they want to review and rename and repaint and do everything they can to remove any trace of Liberal initiatives, Mr. Speaker. However, they should realize that the welfare of our young people is more important than political gain. They should understand that the interests of Canadian youth, of students who will be leaving school in May and June, are more important that the interests of Progressive Conservative flagwavers.
During our term as a government, and my own brief term as Minister of State for Youth, we took some important measures and it did not take five months. We took important measures to respond to the valid concerns of young Canadians.
The First Chance program, designed to provide young people with specialized training, was to have been a highly original and effective way of dealing with the Catch 22: 'No experience, no job-No job, no experience1, facing those entering the labour market for the first time.
Mr. Speaker, this was a $100 million program. The Government took this from under the nose of the Minister of State for Youth, and she saw nothing!
There was a commitment of $1 billion for the next fiscal year, but once again, the Minister of State for Youth said nothing and let this amount pass her by. She has let the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) look after the money in her envelope. I could bet anything, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Employment and Immigration will not use this billion dollars only for young people. Once more, young people will be taken for granted; their concerns will be forgotten, and once again, their unemployment rate will be higher and their hardships worse than those of other Canadians. However, the Minister of State for Youth says that she is taking care of those who are doing well.
January 23, 1985

The proposed young businessmen program, Mr. Speaker, was aimed at meeting the funding needs of small businesses to promote job creation. No one can say that it goes against Conservative principles to help businesses get a start so that jobs will be created. Yet, even this program was axed. But what do they intend to do? Is everything which was faintly Liberal to be eliminated? Are political games going to be played on the backs of young people who want to set up a small business? Will they be left to fend for themselves as they have during the last four months?
Mr. Speaker, you must, like me, have the impression that this Government is trying to save money on the backs of those who need help the most. We know that the Environment 2000 Program-and we know to what extent the Minister of Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) has also been victimized by the cutbacks-was going to create jobs this winter. This program has also been axed.
Mr. Speaker, we must ask ourselves what clout the Minister of State for Youth really has. Is she being used only to make speeches here and there and to offer a few small subsidies? One would have thought we were at a bingo game when she was announcing grants of $5,000 here and $2,000 there!
Mr. Speaker, this is not what will solve the problems of young Canadians now that we have a new government and the same is true of election promises.
I recall that, during the election campaign, they made nothing but promises, promises, and more promises. And I can still remember that, at the Granby Cegep, the Conservative Party made strong commitments about jobs for young people, among other things. Well, now that they have taken over, their only commitment is to slash into every youth-oriented program, Mr. Speaker. I think that the people, particularly young people, are beginning to see the light and will start applying strong pressure on Members opposite to force them to rise and tell the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) to get the job done.
Mr. Speaker, International Youth Year will give us many opportunities to raise the issue of youth over the next few months. Let us just see how that year was inaugurated and what kind of priority this government gives to International Youth Year. For starters, the Minister of State said during the holiday season that she would be making a major statement after the House had resumed. She gets here with a nice little prepared speech, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) butts in and says: If you do not mind, I have a more important statement to make. And the Secretary of State goes on to express his views on the star war, something which young people are dead set against. Once again, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Youth was brushed aside, without getting any press coverage, and that is what she calls a great launching to make the people aware of International Youth Year. But worse, when the Minister of State for Youth took the floor, all the members on that side got up and left. Mr. Speaker, if that is how they show that the problem of
Supply
youth is a priority for them and that International Youth Year will be a meaningful event, in my opinion, it is a very poor performance.
Therefore, it is all very well indeed to have a slogan, to have a grant program, but what we should know is what the Minister announced. She promised some changes, but on reading her speech, all I found was rehashed. She promised grants; the program existed already. The measures to be taken jointly with departments and other federal agencies have already been taken, Mr. Speaker. The program Peace and Development is nothing new. The same goes for the Information and Communication Program. As for the advisory committee, there was one already. The Conservatives preach participation and say that young people should be consulted and involved in the decisions affecting them. The Minister has announced a grant program and various activities that will take place during International Youth Year and yet, her advisory committee has yet to be appointed, Mr. Speaker. Therefore the young must share in the development of whatever concerns them, of the program affecting them, but they are not appointed, Mr. Speaker.
Of course, I am sure that in her travels she has not as yet met all the young Conservatives and that she must wait for the striking committee to give its blessing, Mr. Speaker. But the problem is that all the decisions have been made before an advisory committee has been established. Advising on what, Mr. Speaker? Once more, this is using young Canadians as rubber stamps. The decision have been taken. Hopefully, the young people who are going to sit on that rubber stamp committee will be able to tell the Minister: 'No, we will not rubber-stamp decisions you have already taken.'
Mr. Speaker, if the International Youth Year is going to be more than a slogan, its three themes will have to be considered in a Canadian context. Those themes are: participation, development and peace. The concepts of youth participation and development are of course closely linked. Unfortunately, despite all the attention which the International Youth Year will focus on the concerns of the young, the current situation does not lend itself to youth participation. While more than 500,000 of our young are unemployed, as pointed out by our leader, the prospects for more active involvement of the young in our society are slight indeed. Therefore, if the theme of participation is taken into consideration, we should make sure that we have the means to foster youth participation in our society. And what they want more than anything else, as far as participation is concerned, is to take part in the labour market. Therefore, given the dullness of the speech we just heard, nothing in the remarks of the Minister will enable our youth to have greater access to the labour market. The growth and development of young Canadians depend largely on the training process, self-sufficiency and the dignity of a well-paid job.

January 23, 1985
Supply
Having said that, rather than implementing badly needed training and job creating programs at a time when unemployment could hardly be worse among the young, the new Conservative Government has decided to put an end to the First Opportunity Program which had been very well received, without proposing anything else instead.
As regards participation and development, there are also problems in many other areas. We can, among other things, consider the post-secondary education system. Again, the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) will evade the issue, saying that it falls under the Secretary of State's responsability. But she must admit that even if education comes under provincial jurisdiction, the Federal Government has a very important role to play towards the Established Programs Act. Canadian universities and colleges are underfinanced, which has a negative impact on the quality of our education system and is characterized by drop-outs.
In addition, if she has consulted young people and listened to them, she has certainly heard some evidence about the financial problems of our universities, access to education problems, and I am convinced that the representations she heard should encourage the government to make a renewed effort to help our colleges and universities.
Even worse, she may be aware of those problems but government action does nothing to solve them. In the few months that they have been in power, the Conservatives have already worsened this situation by reducing by $5 million its contribution to the Student Loans Program and by doing away with the important Summer Employment Program, thus denying many other students the possibility of paying for ever-increasing registration costs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, with a theme like "participation", opportunities for participation and youth development are getting scarcer everyday.
Certainly, I could also speak about the issue of peace. Given the nuclear arms race in which both superpowers are engaged, the issue of peace and global stability is very important in the minds of all Canadians, but it particularly haunts young people. Unfortunately, the government of Canada does not seem to recognize nor respect the gallant and legal efforts made by Canadians to bring back peace in the world.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Coates) was quoted in The Toronto Star of December 25 as saying that "The initiatives taken by pacifists do not deserve so much attention". Mr. Speaker, we know that a great number of young people are members of peace movements. The Minister of National Defence insults them publicly. And what happens? The Minister of State for Youth should have taken him to task for it but she did not say a word.
Mr. Speaker, we could mention a host of other initiatives that the Minister of State for Youth should take. She should assume her role. She should certainly make sure that the crisis among young people is not hidden by the good fortune of some
of them; she must address the problems facing the others. Unfortunately, she did not get a mandate from the Government.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the cause of youth has suffered successive setbacks within the Government, particularly because of the insignificance of the role played in Cabinet by the Minister, a person who, in her professional career, was in the limelight, but has now been relegated in the Cabinet to a minor part.
I would like her, Mr. Speaker, to go see the Prime Minister and ask him for a real mandate and some powers to do the job she should normally be doing, and if the Prime Minister refuses to give priority to young people, she should have the courage to do the honourable thing and resign.

Mr. Speaker, it has been quite a day. One can sense the pleading for a return to a system that produced first and second class unemployed Canadians through encouraging politicians to hand out money, much greater amounts of money to ridings which were held by Liberals.
I would encourage the Government to continue the path it has chosen, which is fair and just and does not create first and second class citizens. One gets the feeling in speech after speech by the Liberals that they want to return to the good old days when they were the dispensers of pots of money to their friends and the heck with the rest of Canadians. This Government will not return to those days.
The thrust of the Hon. Member's speech was to make laudatory comments about the Liberal Party and its wisdom in creating the Ministry. If the Hon. Member looks at youth unemployment statistics, he will know that from the time of the defeat of the Conservative Government to 1982, the unemployment rate for youth went up to better than 22 per cent in a little more than a year. Why did it take his Government until 1984 to set up such a Ministry if youth are so important and the Government was so concerned about youth? Why did his Government wait until 1984 when those unemployment rates began to fall? Why did the Liberals not move when the problem was at its height in 1982?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have heard the Hon. Member say that the Government intends to continue in the same direction. If they continue to do what they have been doing since September, they will do nothing at all. And I am sure that an Hon. Member of such high standing as he is would never accept to be part of a government that is doing nothing. For the time being, they are simply going with the tide. We know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration
January 23, 1985

(Miss MacDonald) has announced nothing and done nothing, except hold consultations. We know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is holding consultations too. That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) is holding consultations and making petty arrangements. However, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this Hon. Member with a social conscience would not let 500,000 young Canadians, or whatever the figure is, be without jobs. That is far too many! And it is in this direction that I should like the government to step in. If they really think that their private enterprise can solve the problem overnight or within six months, let it say so!
But, in the meantime, there are young people suffering. The ones on welfare are getting $140 per month.
And when I see the Hon. Member fiddling with the figures,
I must tell him that he is doing it on the backs of the poor. Think in terms of human suffering and not in terms of statistics. There are things to be done, and it is not by doing nothing that you will provide assistance to young people who need it so much.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment to make of course on the comments voiced by the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) and by the Liberals in general. As we would say back home, in Charlevoix, the speech made by the Hon. Member for Shefford does not sound like much and upon closer examination there is not much to it either, for in fact, Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to be doing nothing. Their Government, and that Minister in particular, had every opportunity to do something for our youth, yet young Canadians voted Progressive Conservative on September 4th, and decided to support us. I feel that instead of making lengthy speeches on our youth's needs, we on this side are examining the situation and most of all acting.
Next week in my riding I will have the opportunity to announce two projects in which the Government of Canada is involved and which will create something like a hundred direct jobs. Of course we could spend our time in the House of Commons making lengthy speeches on the needs of our youth which are real. But I feel that instead of attacking the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) who is involved in a consultation process with the Provinces and all the groups concerned, we are getting at much more significant solutions than all your rhetorics ever did over the years.
And how many times during the election campaign did I hear young people complain that they were fed up with these small-time projects from which they could only eke out a meagre living. We are all looking for something else and, together, we will find it, in my own riding we will find a solution.
Your speech, this afternoon, was meaningless from beginning to end. It had no substance at all. In our case, we will take time for reflection. This is what we are doing and the Minister

as well. And we will come forward with concrete proposals provided the cupboard is not entirely bare, which is the situation you left us in. We are now using the financial ress-ources available in the best interests of all Canadians, especially our youth. This is my concern and that of my Government. Therefore nobody is impressed when you are calling for someone's resignation. Besides, you are it seems in no position, according to the polls, to ask for anyone's resignation. If the elections were held today, you would get licked even worse than you were last September 4.
