Talk about insignificance, Mr. Speaker, we have just been given an example. He is talking about a meaningless speech, but the Hon. Member has just shown us that his only claim to glory is to have won the September 4 election. Mr. Speaker, the Member ought to know that winning an election is one thing, but now he must act instead of limiting himself to studying. This is as good a time as any to tell him that if he keeps up that kind of performance he will prove that he does not even know what the Standing Orders are all about. He should beef up on the Standing Orders before making accusations against others. I might add that he will simply confirm that he was elected under false pretenses.
While he is considering and searching, young people in his riding are experiencing problems; they thought he would come up with practical solutions. Well, he does not have much to say to them right now. He keeps his fingers crossed, marking time in the hope that our economic woes will vanish in thin air. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would be well advised to stop playing petty politics at the expense of young people and the Liberals, and he ought to be thankful that we raised the issue of youth in the House, something he has yet to do.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am one of those few on this side who will challenge the handfuls on the other side because even though we are only a handful in this place, we still outnumber them six to one. It is because we were pretty good that we got 211 members elected. Our fellow citizens knew what they were doing. They made their choice, Mr. Speaker.
It came to me as a surprise that the Leader of the Opposition could boldly accuse the government of not having helped the young to secure meaningful and stimulating jobs. He apparently forgot-or may be he dared not to remember-that as recently as a few months ago, his own government had the responsibility to find those meaningful and stimulating jobs. Did that government do anything? Not much.
That government left us a sad legacy of programs not designed to meet the challenges in the workforce, an inconsistent policy that could not resolve past and present problems which have to be tackled in systematic way if we are to give our youth some kind of future. Work creation programs were to be short-term solutions to current problems which are still with us. The former Government knew very well that young Canadians were faced with an extremely high unemployment rate which was not going to disappear overnight. Instead of reaching an agreement with the provinces on the way to deal
with the problems of training young people and creating employment, they prepared for us a very sad legacy: partial agreements, broken promises and no consideration whatsoever for any particular needs, to the point that no co-operation, at any level, seemed possible or even desirable.
The former Government did next to nothing in preparation for the International Youth Year and, to add insult to injury, the small tired group opposite claims that we are following in their footsteps. In their opinion, we are putting too much energy in worthless endeavours instead of dealing with real problems, looking for help from our economic partners and preparing solutions. The present Government has chosen to approach training and development for our youth in a coordinated way. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has just returned from a round of consultations with the provinces and the economic sectors. And she has stated clearly, Mr. Speaker, that the private sector whose views were not recognized by the previous administration expects the federal government and the provinces to prepare in co-operation a coherent national policy on training, retraining and job development. Instead of working in consultation with the provinces to find practical solutions, the previous government took pleasure in acting alone. Therefore federal and provincial programs conflicted with each other and they did not allow for the hope that young people could have one day their place in our country.
Young Canadians, in fact all Canadians, expected more from the federal government. In September, they expressed their total disillusion with that policy of confrontation, and they suggested that they wanted a government determined to co-operate with the provinces. This is what we are doing. Last week, the federal government and the provinces acknowledged the necessity to emphasize co-operation rather than confrontation. This promising start is a tremendous breakthrough as far as federal-provincial co-operation is concerned. The Canadian people hope to see more joint programs implemented and better harmonization of the programs, which could only be to their advantage.
